paras.text: Envelope and Interior: Insulation, Ventilation, Windows and Doors, Finishes, and Specialties, Audio Lecture

This chapter is about fifteen questions on your trade exam. Roughly five on insulation, two on ventilation, five on windows, doors, and skylights, and the rest split between interior finishes and specialty items.

It all comes from the twenty fifteen Michigan Residential Code, not the twenty twenty one code. And this chapter more than any other is where Michigan amended the national numbers. That is not a footnote, it is the exam's whole strategy here. The wrong answer will usually be the correct national number.
So listen for the phrase Michigan amendment, and when you hear it, say the Michigan number twice and the national number once, labeled as the trap.
Idea one. The three Michigan climate zones.
Michigan has three, and you need to know which one a city is in.
Zone five A is the southern Lower Peninsula. Detroit, Grand Rapids, Lansing. That is where you live and work, so that is the zone most of your questions will describe.
Zone six A is the northern Lower Peninsula and the eastern Upper Peninsula.
Zone seven is the western U P, the coldest part of the state.
Now the single most important Michigan amendment in this chapter. In zone five A, the ceiling insulation requirement is R thirty eight.
The national energy code says R forty nine for zone five. Michigan amended it down to thirty eight.

So if the question says southern Michigan, or names a southern city, the answer is R thirty eight, and R forty nine is the trap. Up in zones six A and seven, northern Michigan and the U P, the ceiling really is R forty nine.
South thirty eight, north forty nine. Say it back.
Idea two. The rest of the insulation table.
Walls are easier, because they are the same statewide. R twenty in the cavity, or R thirteen cavity plus R five continuous insulated sheathing on the outside.
Floors over unconditioned space are R thirty, except zone seven where they rise to R thirty eight.
Basement walls. In zone five A you need R ten continuous or R thirteen cavity. In zones six A and seven it is R fifteen continuous or R nineteen cavity.

Now here is a reading skill that is worth a point by itself. When you see two numbers with a slash, like ten slash thirteen, the first number is always continuous insulation, meaning rigid foam on the face, and the second is cavity insulation in a framed wall. Either one complies. It is not a sum, it is a choice.
Slab edges get R ten in every zone. What changes is the depth. Two feet down in zone five A, four feet down in six A and seven.
Idea three. Windows, and two numbers that are not the national ones.
The maximum window U factor in Michigan is zero point three two, in every zone.
Not zero point three zero. That is the twenty twenty one national number and it is not in force here.
Skylights get zero point five five.
And keep the direction straight, because U factor runs backward from R value. Lower is better, because U factor is one divided by R. A big R is good, a small U is good.

One more giveaway, and it is an easy point when you spot it. There is no solar heat gain requirement in Michigan. S H G C limits are for hot southern climates. If a Michigan question offers you a solar heat gain number, it is a trap, because the table says not required.
Idea four. Air leakage, another Michigan amendment.
The maximum is four air changes per hour at fifty pascals, verified with a mandatory blower door test.
The model code says three. Michigan says four. Four is your answer.
Hold onto that number, because it comes back in a few minutes and connects to something else.
Idea five. Vapor retarders, which installers get wrong in real life.
In climate zones five, six, and seven, which is all of Michigan, you need a Class one or Class two vapor retarder on the interior side of frame walls.
Interior means the warm in winter side. That is the principle, and if you hold it, you can reason out the rest.

The three classes, by permeability. Class one is poly sheeting or foil facing, a tenth of a perm or less. Class two is kraft faced batts, up to one perm. Class three is just latex paint, up to ten perms.

Class three is only allowed when the wall can dry, and there are two ways to earn it. Either vented cladding over the sheathing, or enough continuous insulated sheathing to keep the wall warm, which is R five over a two by four wall in zone five, and R seven and a half over a two by six.
And now the rule that is worth saying out loud twice. Never put poly on the outside of a Michigan wall.

Here is why, because the reason makes it stick. You already have a required vapor retarder on the inside. Add poly on the outside and you have built a double vapor barrier. Moisture gets into that wall, and then it cannot dry in either direction. That is rot and mold, and on the exam it is a wrong answer every single time.
Question. Where does the vapor retarder go in a Michigan wall, and what happens if you also wrap the outside in poly.
On the interior side, the warm in winter side. Poly on the outside creates a double vapor barrier that traps moisture with no drying path, which is rot.
Idea six. Insulation odds and ends.
R values per inch, roughly. Fiberglass batts about R three point two per inch. Blown cellulose about three point five. Extruded polystyrene about five. Closed cell spray foam six or better.

And one performance fact that is really a job site fact. Compressing a batt into a smaller cavity lowers its R value. An R nineteen squeezed into a two by four wall performs like R thirteen. You do not get nineteen just because the label says nineteen.
At the eaves, insulation baffles must hold a one inch minimum air space between the insulation and the roof sheathing, so ventilation air can actually move.
Idea seven. Attic ventilation, and the arithmetic.
The base rule is one to one fifty. Net free vent area equal to one one hundred fiftieth of the attic floor area.
You can cut that in half, to one three hundredth, if either of two conditions is met.
Condition one, a Class one or two vapor retarder on the warm side of the ceiling. But that only counts in climate zones six and seven, not in zone five A.
Condition two, forty to fifty percent of the vent area placed high in the attic, within three feet of the ridge measured vertically, with the rest down at the eaves.
Either condition alone is enough.
Quick math so the ratio is not abstract. A fifteen hundred square foot attic at one to three hundred needs five square feet of net free area. At one to one fifty it needs ten.
Idea eight. Mechanical ventilation, and two pairs of numbers.
The exam swaps these constantly, so learn them as a pair with a reason.
Bathrooms, fifty C F M intermittent, or twenty continuous.
Kitchens, one hundred C F M intermittent, or twenty five continuous.
Bigger room load, bigger number. The kitchen gets a hundred because you are boiling water and searing food in it.

And an absolute rule. Every exhaust fan discharges outdoors. Never into the attic, never into a soffit, never into a crawl space. Dumping moist air into an attic breeds mold and feeds ice dams, which in Michigan means you built the problem you will be back to fix.
Now the connection question they like, and this is where that four comes back.
Whole house mechanical ventilation is required whenever the blower door test comes in under five air changes per hour. Michigan requires every new house to test at four or tighter.
So follow the logic. Four is tighter than five. Which means every new Michigan home needs whole house mechanical ventilation. Not most. Every one.
A typical rate for a house between fifteen hundred and three thousand square feet with two or three bedrooms is sixty C F M continuous.

One specialty item rides along here. Radon. The E P A action level is four picocuries per liter. The standard new construction answer is a passive sub slab depressurization system, meaning a four inch gravel layer under the slab, a poly soil gas retarder, and a three to four inch vent pipe running from under the slab straight up through the roof, with power roughed in for a future fan.
Question. Why does every new Michigan house need whole house mechanical ventilation.

Because whole house ventilation is triggered under five air changes per hour, and Michigan's own air leakage limit requires every new house to test at four or tighter. The tightness rule guarantees the ventilation rule.
Idea nine. Egress windows, which is the heart of the window questions.
Emergency escape and rescue openings are required in every sleeping room, in basements with habitable space, and in habitable attics.
Four numbers, and they are the ones to burn in.
Five point seven square feet of net clear opening. Five point zero if it is a grade floor opening.
Minimum clear height twenty four inches. Minimum clear width twenty inches. Maximum sill height forty four inches above the floor.
And it has to open from inside without keys, tools, or special knowledge.
Now the classic trick, and it is a genuinely good question. A window at exactly twenty inches wide and twenty four inches high is only three point three three square feet.

Do that multiplication in your head. Twenty times twenty four is four hundred eighty square inches, and there are one hundred forty four square inches in a square foot, so that is three point three three.
So meeting both minimum dimensions does not meet the area. One dimension has to be bigger than its minimum. That is the point of the question.

If the egress window is below grade, the window well needs nine square feet of horizontal area with thirty six inches in each direction. And if the well is deeper than forty four inches, it needs a permanent ladder or steps.
Idea ten. Safety glazing, section R three oh eight point four.
Tempered glass is required in hazardous locations, and the list is worth learning as locations rather than as numbers.
All glass in doors.
Glass within a twenty four inch arc of either side of a closed door, when the bottom edge is under sixty inches above the floor.

Big panes that meet all four of these together. Over nine square feet. Bottom edge under eighteen inches from the floor. Top edge over thirty six inches. And a walking surface within thirty six inches. All four, not any one.
Glass in guards and railings, always, no exceptions.
Wet locations. Any glass with a bottom edge less than sixty inches above a tub or shower drain and within sixty inches horizontally of the water. Sixty, not seventy two.
And stairways. Glass within thirty six inches horizontally of a walking surface and under sixty inches above it, plus glass within sixty inches of the bottom tread.
Tempered panes carry a permanent etched label. No label, no pass. That is how an inspector calls it, and it is how the exam calls it.
Idea eleven. Three door and window rules.

Window fall protection. If an operable window's sill is less than twenty four inches above the floor inside, and the drop outside is more than seventy two inches, then the opening cannot pass a four inch sphere, or it needs an approved opening control device.
Twenty four inside, seventy two outside. A low sill over a long drop.
Every house needs at least one side hinged exterior egress door with thirty two inches of clear width and seventy eight inches of clear height.

And the door from an attached garage into the house. One and three eighths inch solid wood, one and three eighths solid or honeycomb core steel, or a twenty minute fire rated door. Self closing. And it may never open into a bedroom.
Idea twelve. Drywall, and the garage separation that is nearly guaranteed.
Fastener spacing without adhesive. Ceilings take nails every seven inches or screws every twelve. Walls take nails every eight or screws every sixteen.
Ceilings are always tighter, and the reason is gravity. That is your check if you cannot remember which is which.
Screws have to bite five eighths of an inch into the wood.
Half inch board is standard on walls and on ceilings framed sixteen inches on center. At twenty four inches on center, ceilings step up to five eighths, or half inch sag resistant board.
Type X is the fire rated core. Type C is the upgraded fire rated core that outperforms X.
Now the garage separation, which shows up on this exam somewhere almost every time.
Walls between the garage and the house get half inch gypsum on the garage side. Every wall, always.
The ceiling of a garage with living space above it gets five eighths Type X.
Structure supporting that floor gets half inch.
The trap runs in both directions, so watch it. Type X on the walls is wrong. And plain half inch on a ceiling under a bedroom is wrong.

And one more thing they test. This is a separation, not a rated assembly. If an answer choice says one hour fire wall, that is the trap. The code calls for separation materials, and it never requires an hour rating for a house garage.
Ducts passing through the separation must be twenty six gauge steel with no openings into the garage.
Question. Garage with a bedroom above it. What goes on the garage side walls, and what goes on the garage ceiling.
Half inch gypsum on the walls. Five eighths Type X on the ceiling because there is living space above. And it is a separation, not a one hour rated wall.
Idea thirteen. Finish levels and wet areas, which is your second pass on both.

Drywall finish levels, zero through five. Level one, tape embedded, for plenums. Level two, tape plus one coat, for garages and behind tile. Level three, two coats, for heavy texture. Level four, three coats, standard for flat paint. Level five adds a skim coat over the whole surface, for gloss, semi gloss, and critical lighting.
Wet areas. Tub and shower walls need a nonabsorbent finish to six feet above the floor.

Tile in wet areas goes over cement board, fiber cement, or glass mat gypsum. Never paper faced green board. And it is set with thinset, the cement mortar. Mastic is for dry walls only, because it softens in moisture and fails.
Idea fourteen. The specialties, four quick items.

Attic access is required when the attic is over thirty square feet with thirty inches or more of height. The rough opening is twenty two by thirty inches, located in a hallway or other accessible spot, with thirty inches of headroom above the hatch.
Memory hook, thirty, thirty, thirty, through a twenty two by thirty opening.
Smoke alarms. In every bedroom, outside every sleeping area, and on every story including the basement. All interconnected, hardwired, with battery backup.

Carbon monoxide alarms. The trigger is a fuel burning appliance or an attached garage. The location is outside each sleeping area. And here is the discriminator, under the twenty fifteen code they do not have to interconnect. Interconnection is a smoke alarm rule.
Pool barriers. Forty eight inches high, no opening that passes a four inch sphere, and a self closing self latching gate with the latch at fifty four inches or on the pool side.
Rapid fire recap. Say these with me.

Ceiling insulation, R thirty eight south, R forty nine north. Walls, R twenty, or thirteen plus five. Basement, ten thirteen south, fifteen nineteen north. Slab, R ten, two feet south, four feet north. Window U factor, point three two. Skylight, point five five. Air leakage, four A C H fifty with a blower door test. Vapor retarder, Class one or two, interior side. Attic vents, one to one fifty, or one to three hundred. Baffle air space, one inch. Bath fan, fifty and twenty. Kitchen fan, one hundred and twenty five. Whole house trigger, under five A C H fifty. Egress, five point seven square feet, five point zero at grade, twenty four high, twenty wide, forty four sill. Window well, nine square feet, thirty six inches, ladder past forty four deep. Tempered glass, twenty four inch door arc under sixty, nine square feet with eighteen and thirty six and thirty six, sixty above the drain, thirty six and sixty at stairs. Fall protection, sill under twenty four inside, drop over seventy two outside, four inch sphere. Egress door, thirty two by seventy eight clear. Garage door to house, one and three eighths, self closing, never into a bedroom. Garage gypsum, half inch walls, five eighths Type X ceiling. Drywall fasteners, seven and twelve on ceilings, eight and sixteen on walls. Screws, five eighths bite. Tub walls, nonabsorbent to six feet. Attic access, twenty two by thirty, thirty square feet, thirty inches headroom. Radon, four picocuries per liter.

Fifteen questions here. The three I would drill hardest are R thirty eight for southern Michigan, because the national R forty nine is sitting right there as bait, the egress numbers including why twenty by twenty four fails, and the garage separation in both directions. Those three carry the chapter.
